original_question: Of the three genes that, when mutated, cause a metabolic disease resulting in the body producing an odor similar to tyrosinemia, the gene coding for the longest of these proteins is located on which chromosome?

final_qi.question: Of the three genes that, when mutated, cause a metabolic disease resulting in the body producing an odor similar to tyrosinemia, the gene coding for the longest of these proteins is located on which chromosome?
final_qi.long_answer: The metabolic disease is isolated hypermethioninemia, which can be produced by pathogenic variants in three different genes: MAT1A, GNMT and AHCY. Among the proteins they encode, adenosyl-homocysteine hydrolase (AHCY) is the longest (≈430 amino acids). The human AHCY gene is situated on chromosome 20 (cytogenetic band 20q11.22), so the longest-protein gene of the three resides on chromosome 20.

final_answer.long_answer: Isolated hypermethioninemia (which gives a boiled-cabbage/fishy odor like tyrosinemia) can result from pathogenic variants in three genes: MAT1A, GNMT and AHCY. The proteins they encode are ~395, 292 and 432 amino acids long, respectively. The longest of these is S-adenosyl-homocysteine hydrolase (encoded by AHCY), whose gene is situated at 20q13.2 on chromosome 20.

1.question: Which of those three genes codes for the longest protein?
1.search_keyword: longest protein gene among three genes

final_answer.long_answer: The metabolic disorder multiple-acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency (glutaric acidemia type II) gives patients a rancid/fish-like body odour that resembles the smell noted in tyrosinemia. Pathogenic variants in any of three genes—ETFA, ETFB, and ETFDH—can cause this disease. Of these, ETFDH encodes the longest protein (≈600 amino acids). The ETFDH gene is located on chromosome 4 (band 4q32–q34), so the longest-protein gene of the three is found on chromosome 4.
